In this section of *HEA 4 Money Web*, the teaching focuses on direct observation of the mind: *"I thought Buddhists didn’t believe in money.’ The usual response is something along the lines of, ‘Well, that’s not quite the way it works.’ As Buddhist monks and nuns we don’t use or accept money, that’s true, we don’t own money – I haven’t used money since 1978 – but only a very small proportion of Buddhists are monastics, most Buddhists are ordinary householders."* The central guidance is to step back from the habitual impulse to control or fix present experience, and instead cultivate a spacious, non-reactive presence. When we investigate thoughts and feelings without identification (*anattā*), their grip on the heart naturally dissolves. It is like It is like a small boat floating on a calm mountain lake beneath an open sky. Rest in that clear, unentangled knowing.

In 'HEA 4 Money Web' (Chapter 1), how should a meditator handle restless thoughts and mental chatter?

The text reflects: *"In one teaching he says one whose mind is obsessed with gain, honour and praise is like a dung beetle, ‘a dung-eater, stuffed with dung’ (S 17.5), that collects dung to make it into a big ball."* Thoughts are merely passing mental formations (*saṅkhāra*); they have no solid core unless we feed them with belief. When a thought arises, simply recognize it as 'thinking, thinking' without jumping into the storyline. It is like It is like an anchor dropped deep into the seabed, keeping the boat steady in stormy waves. Be the vast, open sky through which thoughts pass like harmless clouds.
